content: In recent years, it has become evident that some carriers are either refusing to transport certain goods or imposing additional conditions for their carriage. As long as these conditions do not violate legal requirements, such actions are not considered illegal. Both the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) and the International Air Transport Association (IATA) provide lists of the primary restrictions imposed by airlines. Some airlines completely prohibit the transport of dangerous goods, while others allow only a very limited range of such items. Since carrier restrictions for different modes of transport are not centrally published, it is crucial to ensure harmonization among all stakeholders involved. The shipper (sender or consignor) has specific responsibilities, including: Making prior arrangements with the receiver, such as determining the need for import/export permits. Coordinating with the carrier to ensure the shipment is accepted for appropriate transport and, if possible, arranging for direct transport via the most direct route. Preparing all necessary documentation, including permits, dispatch, and shipping documents. Informing the receiver of the transportation arrangements well in advance of the expected arrival time. The carrier is responsible for: Advising the sender on the required shipping documents and providing instructions for their completion. Offering guidance on proper packaging. Assisting the sender in arranging the most direct routing and confirming the routing details. Maintaining and archiving all shipment and transport documentation. The receiver (consignee) must: Obtain the necessary authorizations from national authorities for the importation of the material. Provide the sender with the required import permits, letters of authorization, or other documents mandated by national authorities. Arrange for the timely and efficient collection of the shipment upon arrival. Acknowledge receipt of the shipment to the sender. Shipments should not be dispatched until: Advance arrangements have been made between the sender, carrier, and receiver. The shipper has confirmed with national authorities that the material can be legally exported. The receiver has confirmed with national authorities that the material can be legally imported. The receiver has ensured that there will be no delays in delivering the package to its destination. For air mail, infectious substances in Category A are not accepted for shipment through postal services. However, Category B infectious substances may be shipped via registered air mail, following the Universal Postal Union's recommended procedures. The triple packaging system must be used, adhering to the same requirements as for other transport methods. The address label must display the word Letter and include the green Customs Declaration Label for international mail. The package must also be marked with the white diamond label bearing the text UN 3373 for Biological Substance, Category B. Local and international restrictions may apply, so prior contact with the national postal operator is necessary to confirm acceptance of the packaged material. In the event of exposure to infectious substances, the affected area should be washed or disinfected immediately, regardless of the agent involved. If the substance comes into contact with non-intact skin, washing with soap and water or an antiseptic solution can reduce the risk of infection. Medical advice should be sought whenever there is suspected exposure to infectious substances due to a damaged package. A trained individual should follow these steps for spill cleanup: 1. Wear gloves and protective clothing, including face and eye protection if necessary. 2. Cover the spill with a cloth or paper towels to contain it. 3. Pour an appropriate disinfectant over the cloth or towels and the surrounding area (e.g., 5% bleach solution or quaternary ammonium disinfectants for aircraft spills). 4. Apply the disinfectant concentrically, starting from the outer edge of the spill and working toward the center. 5. After 30 minutes, remove the materials. If broken glass or sharps are involved, use a dustpan or stiff cardboard to collect them and place them in a puncture-resistant container for disposal. 6. Clean and disinfect the spill area, repeating steps 2–5 if necessary. 7. Dispose of contaminated materials in a leak-proof, puncture-resistant waste disposal container. 8. After successful disinfection, report the incident to the competent authority and inform them that the site has been decontaminated. Incident reporting is required for both Categories A and B infectious substances, particularly for Category A. Reports must be submitted to the relevant transport and health authorities. While no documented infections have resulted from transport-related exposures (except for the 2001 anthrax letters in the USA), there have been reports of respiratory infections and tuberculosis transmission associated with air travel, attributed to direct person-to-person contact rather than packaging or shipping issues. Statistical data from central laboratories demonstrate the effectiveness of compliant packaging (e.g., P650 and P620) in preventing leakage and material loss during transport. Only 0.002% of shipments experienced leakage, all of which were contained by absorbent materials without damage to secondary containers or outer packaging. The United Nations provides comprehensive guidelines for the transport of dangerous goods, including infectious substances. These guidelines are available for download in PDF format and include specific provisions for air transport, highlighted in grey. Packing instructions, such as P620 and P650, outline the requirements for packaging infectious substances to ensure safety during transport. For example, P620 applies to UN 2814 and UN 2900, requiring leak-proof primary and secondary packaging, absorbent material, and rigid outer packaging. Additional requirements include maintaining packaging integrity under specific temperature and pressure conditions and ensuring proper labeling and documentation. Shippers must ensure that packages are prepared to arrive in good condition and pose no hazard during transport. An itemized list of contents must be enclosed between the secondary and outer packaging. If the infectious substances are unknown but suspected to meet Category A criteria, the phrase suspected Category A infectious substance must be included in the documentation. Empty packaging must be disinfected or sterilized before reuse, and any labels indicating previous infectious contents must be removed or obliterated.
